questions.question: What is dynamic programming and when do you use it?
questions.title: Dynamic Programming Introduction Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Dynamic programming (DP)** solves problems by breaking them into **overlapping subproblems** and **storing each subproblem's answer** so it's computed only once. Use it when the problem has **optimal substructure** (the optimum is built from sub-optima) **and overlapping subproblems** (the same subproblem recurs). It turns exponential recursion into **polynomial** time, via **memoization** (top-down) or **tabulation** (bottom-up).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can name the two preconditions (overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure) and the two implementation styles
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling any recursion 'DP', or applying DP without overlapping subproblems (then it's just divide-and-conquer)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Contrast naive O(2^n) Fibonacci with memoized O(n) and name the two preconditions explicitly

sections.title: What Dynamic Programming Is
sections.content:
**Dynamic programming** is an optimization technique for problems that have two properties. **Overlapping subproblems**: the recursive solution solves the **same** smaller problems repeatedly (naive Fibonacci recomputes `fib(3)` many times). **Optimal substructure**: an optimal solution to the whole is built from optimal solutions to its parts.

When both hold, DP **stores each subproblem's result once** and reuses it, collapsing exponential recursion into **polynomial** time. Two styles: **memoization** (top-down recursion + a cache) and **tabulation** (bottom-up, fill a table from base cases up). If a problem has optimal substructure but **no** overlap, it's plain **divide-and-conquer** (like merge sort), not DP.

sections.title: Naive Recursion vs DP
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[problem] --> B{overlapping
subproblems?} B -- no --> C[divide & conquer
not DP] B -- yes --> D{optimal
substructure?} D -- no --> E[greedy / other] D -- yes --> F[DP: store each
subproblem once] F --> G[memoization
top-down + cache] F --> H[tabulation
bottom-up table] ```

sections.title: Fibonacci: Exponential vs DP
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling all recursion DP**: DP specifically requires **overlapping subproblems**.
- **No overlap**: if subproblems don't repeat, you don't need caching - it's divide-and-conquer.
- **Wrong state definition**: a bad `dp[i]` meaning leads to incorrect transitions - define state first.
- **Ignoring base cases**: tabulation must seed the table; memoization must have a base return.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- DP needs **overlapping subproblems** + **optimal substructure**.
- It **stores each subproblem once** -> polynomial instead of exponential.
- **Memoization** = top-down + cache; **Tabulation** = bottom-up table.
- No overlap -> it's **divide-and-conquer**, not DP.
- Start by defining the **state** and the **transition**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Dynamic programming is an optimization technique for problems that break into subproblems, but with two specific properties. The first is overlapping subproblems, meaning a naive recursive solution would solve the same smaller problem over and over. The textbook example is Fibonacci, where computing fib of n recursively recomputes fib of three, fib of two, and so on, an exponential number of times. The second property is optimal substructure, meaning the optimal solution to the whole problem is built from optimal solutions to its subproblems. When both properties hold, the core DP idea is to compute each distinct subproblem only once and store its answer, so I never recompute it. That single change collapses exponential recursion into polynomial time. For Fibonacci, the naive version is O of two to the n, but once I store results it becomes O of n. There are two ways to implement DP. Memoization is top-down: I keep the natural recursion but add a cache, and before computing a subproblem I check whether it's already in the cache. Tabulation is bottom-up: I fill a table starting from the base cases and build up to the answer, often letting me drop space down to constant. A point I'd make to show understanding is that not every recursion is DP. If the subproblems don't actually overlap, like in merge sort, then there's nothing to cache and it's just divide-and-conquer. So when I approach a DP problem, I first define the state, what dp of i means, then the transition between states, then the base cases.

questions.question: How do you solve the coin change problem using dynamic programming?
questions.title: Coin Change DP Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Coin change (min coins)**: find the fewest coins summing to an amount. Define `dp[a]` = minimum coins to make amount `a`. Transition: `dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - coin])` over all coins `<= a`. Base `dp[0] = 0`; initialize the rest to a large sentinel (infinity). Build bottom-up to `dp[amount]`. **O(amount * coins)** time, **O(amount)** space; return -1 if unreachable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you define the dp state, the min-over-coins transition, and the unreachable (-1) case
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Greedily picking the largest coin (fails for coins like {1,3,4}, amount 6), or wrong base/sentinel
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why greedy fails and how the dp[0]=0 base plus an infinity sentinel handles unreachable amounts

sections.title: Coin Change with DP
sections.content:
Given coin denominations and a target `amount`, find the **minimum number of coins** that sum to it. **Greedy (always take the biggest coin) fails** for many coin sets - e.g. coins `{1, 3, 4}`, amount `6`: greedy gives `4+1+1 = 3` coins, but the optimum is `3+3 = 2`. So you need DP.

Define **`dp[a]`** = the minimum coins to make amount `a`. The transition tries each coin: `dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - coin])` for every coin `<= a`. Seed **`dp[0] = 0`** (zero coins make zero) and set the rest to a large **sentinel** (representing 'unreachable / infinity'). Fill the table from `1` up to `amount`. If `dp[amount]` is still the sentinel, return **-1**. Time **O(amount * #coins)**, space **O(amount)**.

sections.title: Coin Change DP Build
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[dp 0 = 0
dp 1..amount = INF] --> B{for a = 1..amount} B --> C{for each coin <= a} C --> D[dp a = min dp a, 1 + dp a-coin] D --> C C -- done --> B B -- done --> E{dp amount == INF?} E -- yes --> F[return -1] E -- no --> G[return dp amount] ```

sections.title: Min Coins with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Greedy**: picking the largest coin first is wrong for non-canonical coin systems.
- **Bad sentinel**: use `amount + 1` (always > any real answer) so `min` works and unreachable is detectable.
- **Wrong base**: `dp[0]` must be 0, not the sentinel.
- **Confusing variants**: 'min coins' (this) vs 'number of ways' (different transition, sum not min).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`dp[a]`** = min coins for amount `a`.
- Transition: `dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - coin])`.
- Base **`dp[0] = 0`**, rest = sentinel (infinity).
- Unreachable amount -> return **-1**.
- **Greedy fails**; DP is needed. O(amount * #coins).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Coin change asks for the minimum number of coins that add up to a target amount. The first thing I'd point out is why a greedy approach, always grabbing the largest coin that fits, doesn't work in general. With coins one, three, and four, making six greedily gives four plus one plus one, three coins, but the real optimum is three plus three, just two coins. So I use dynamic programming. I define dp of a as the minimum number of coins needed to make amount a. The transition is: for each amount a, I try every coin that's less than or equal to a, and dp of a is one plus the minimum of dp of a minus that coin. The one accounts for using that one coin, and dp of a minus coin is the best way to make the remaining amount. The base case is dp of zero equals zero, because it takes no coins to make zero. I initialize all the other entries to a large sentinel value, like amount plus one, which stands in for infinity, meaning unreachable. Then I fill the table bottom-up from one to the target. At the end, if dp of the amount is still that sentinel, the amount can't be made with the given coins, so I return minus one; otherwise I return dp of amount. The complexity is O of amount times the number of coins, with O of amount space. One clarification I'd make is that this is the minimum-coins variant; there's a related problem asking for the number of distinct ways to make the amount, which uses a summing transition instead of a min.

questions.question: What is the longest common subsequence (LCS) problem?
questions.title: Longest Common Subsequence LCS Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **LCS** finds the longest sequence appearing in both strings **in order but not necessarily contiguous**. Use a 2D table where `dp[i][j]` = LCS length of the first `i` chars of A and first `j` of B. If `A[i-1] == B[j-1]`, `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1`; else `max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])`. **O(m*n)** time and space.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you set up the 2D dp, the match vs no-match transition, and distinguish subsequence from substring
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing subsequence (non-contiguous) with substring (contiguous), or off-by-one with 1-indexed dp
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note the match transition uses the diagonal +1 and that LCS underlies diff tools and edit distance

sections.title: Longest Common Subsequence
sections.content:
A **subsequence** keeps characters **in order** but allows gaps (unlike a **substring**, which must be contiguous). **LCS** finds the longest subsequence common to two strings A (length m) and B (length n) - e.g. LCS of `ABCBDAB` and `BDCAB` is `BCAB` (length 4).

Use a **2D DP table**: `dp[i][j]` = the LCS length of the first `i` characters of A and first `j` of B (1-indexed for clean base cases of 0). Transition: if the current characters **match** (`A[i-1] == B[j-1]`), extend the diagonal: `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1`. If they **don't**, take the best of dropping one character from either: `max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])`. Answer is `dp[m][n]`. **O(m*n)** time and space (reducible to O(n) space).

sections.title: LCS Transition
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[dp i j] --> B{A i-1 == B j-1?} B -- yes --> C[dp i j = dp i-1 j-1 + 1
diagonal + 1] B -- no --> D[dp i j = max
dp i-1 j, dp i j-1] C --> Z[answer = dp m n] D --> Z ```

sections.title: LCS with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Subsequence vs substring**: LCS allows **gaps**; substring must be contiguous (different DP).
- **Off-by-one**: with 1-indexed dp, compare `a.charAt(i-1)` and `b.charAt(j-1)`.
- **Forgetting base row/column**: `dp[0][*]` and `dp[*][0]` are 0.
- **Wrong no-match transition**: it's `max` of the two neighbors, not the diagonal.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Subsequence = in order, **gaps allowed** (not contiguous).
- `dp[i][j]` = LCS length of A[0..i) and B[0..j).
- **Match** -> `dp[i-1][j-1] + 1`; **no match** -> `max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])`.
- Answer `dp[m][n]`; **O(m*n)** time/space (O(n) space possible).
- Foundation of **diff tools** and edit distance.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: First I'd clarify what a subsequence is, because that's the common confusion. A subsequence keeps the characters in their original order but allows gaps, so it doesn't have to be contiguous, unlike a substring which does. The longest common subsequence problem asks for the longest sequence that appears in both strings as a subsequence. I solve it with a two-dimensional DP table. I define dp of i, j as the length of the LCS of the first i characters of string A and the first j characters of string B. I use one-based indexing for the table so that the base cases, an empty prefix on either side, are naturally zero. The transition has two cases. If the current characters match, that is A at i minus one equals B at j minus one, then I extend the LCS by taking the diagonal value and adding one: dp of i minus one, j minus one, plus one. If they don't match, I can't extend, so I take the best I can get by dropping one character from either string: the max of dp of i minus one, j and dp of i, j minus one. The answer is in dp of m, n. The complexity is O of m times n in both time and space, though I can reduce the space to O of n by keeping only the previous row, since each cell only depends on the row above and the current row. I'd also mention that LCS is the foundation of diff tools that compare files and it's closely related to edit distance, which is another classic DP.

questions.question: How do you solve the 0/1 knapsack problem using dynamic programming?
questions.title: 01 Knapsack Problem DP Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **0/1 knapsack**: pick items (each used **at most once**) to maximize value within a weight **capacity**. `dp[i][w]` = max value using the first `i` items with capacity `w`. For each item, choose the better of **skip** (`dp[i-1][w]`) or **take** (`dp[i-1][w - wt] + val`, if it fits). **O(n*W)** time; reducible to **O(W)** space by iterating weight **backwards**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you set up the take/skip transition and know the 0/1 (each item once) constraint and backward 1D optimization
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Allowing item reuse (that's unbounded knapsack), or iterating weight forward in the 1D version (which reuses items)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why the 1D rolling array must iterate weight in reverse to enforce 'each item once'

sections.title: 0/1 Knapsack with DP
sections.content:
In **0/1 knapsack**, each item is either **taken once or left** (no fractions, no repeats), and you maximize total **value** without exceeding a weight **capacity W**. Define **`dp[i][w]`** = the maximum value achievable using the first `i` items with capacity `w`.

For item `i`, you have two choices: **skip** it (`dp[i-1][w]`) or **take** it if it fits (`dp[i-1][w - weight[i]] + value[i]`). Take the max. Base case: zero items -> value 0. The full table is **O(n*W)** time and space. A common optimization uses a **1D array** `dp[w]`, but you must iterate `w` **from high to low** - iterating forward would let the same item be counted multiple times (that would be **unbounded** knapsack).

sections.title: Take or Skip Each Item
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[dp i w] --> B{weight i <= w?} B -- no --> C[skip:
dp i w = dp i-1 w] B -- yes --> D[dp i w = max
skip dp i-1 w,
take dp i-1 w-wt + val] C --> Z[answer = dp n W] D --> Z ```

sections.title: 0/1 Knapsack (1D, Backward) with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Allowing reuse**: taking an item multiple times is **unbounded** knapsack, a different problem.
- **Forward 1D loop**: iterating `w` ascending in the 1D version reuses the same item - must go **backward**.
- **Fractional items**: 0/1 forbids fractions (that's fractional knapsack, solved greedily).
- **Off-by-one on capacity**: only `take` when `weight[i] <= w`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- 0/1 = each item **taken once or skipped**.
- `dp[i][w] = max(skip, take if it fits)`.
- **O(n*W)** time; **O(W)** space with a 1D array.
- 1D array must iterate weight **backward** to enforce 0/1.
- Reuse allowed -> unbounded; fractions allowed -> fractional (greedy).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: In the zero-one knapsack problem, I have a set of items, each with a weight and a value, and a knapsack with a maximum weight capacity. Each item can either be taken once or left out entirely, no fractions and no repeats, and I want to maximize the total value without exceeding the capacity. I define dp of i, w as the maximum value I can achieve using the first i items with a capacity of w. For each item, I have two choices. I can skip it, in which case the value is dp of i minus one, w, the best I could do with the previous items and the same capacity. Or, if the item fits, I can take it, which gives its value plus dp of i minus one, w minus the item's weight, the best I could do with the remaining capacity using the earlier items. I take the maximum of those two. The base case is zero items giving zero value. The full two-dimensional table is O of n times W in both time and space. A nice optimization is to collapse it to a one-dimensional array indexed by weight, but there's a critical detail: I have to iterate the weight from high to low, backwards. If I went forward, then dp of w minus the weight would already reflect the current item, which would effectively let me use the same item multiple times, and that turns it into the unbounded knapsack problem. Iterating backward keeps dp of w minus weight referring to the previous item's state, correctly enforcing the take-each-item-once rule. I'd also distinguish this from fractional knapsack, where you can take fractions of items, which is solved greedily by value-to-weight ratio rather than with DP.

questions.question: What is memoization vs tabulation in DP and which should you use in interviews?
questions.title: Memoization vs Tabulation in Dynamic Programming
questions.direct_answer: **Memoization** is **top-down**: write the natural recursion and **cache** each subproblem's result. **Tabulation** is **bottom-up**: fill a **table** iteratively from base cases up to the answer. Memoization is **easier to write** and only computes **needed** subproblems; tabulation avoids recursion overhead/stack overflow and enables **space optimization**. Both are **O(states * work)**; pick memoization for clarity, tabulation for performance/space.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can contrast the two DP styles on direction, ease, and stack/space tradeoffs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking they have different time complexity, or that one is 'real DP' and the other isn't
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note memoization computes only reachable states while tabulation enables O(1)/rolling-array space

sections.title: Memoization vs Tabulation
sections.content:
Both are ways to implement dynamic programming; they have the **same time complexity** but differ in **direction and tradeoffs**.

**Memoization (top-down)**: keep the intuitive **recursion** but store each subproblem's answer in a cache (array/map); before computing, check the cache. It's **easy to write** from the recurrence and only ever computes the subproblems actually **reached**. **Tabulation (bottom-up)**: define an iterative order and fill a **table** from base cases up to the target, no recursion. It **avoids call-stack overhead and stack-overflow** risk on deep inputs, and often enables **space optimization** (rolling array -> O(1)/O(n)). In interviews: start with memoization for clarity, convert to tabulation if you need the performance or reduced space.

sections.title: Top-Down vs Bottom-Up
sections.content:
blue|Memoization|~top-down recursion|cache each result|computes only needed states|easy from the recurrence
emerald|Tabulation|~bottom-up table|iterative fill|no recursion overhead|enables space optimization
amber|Same time|~O states * work|both avoid recompute|differ in constants|not different Big-O
rose|Pick by|~clarity vs performance|memo for quick coding|tab for deep inputs / space|tab avoids stack overflow

sections.title: Memoization vs Tabulation
sections.content:
| Aspect | Memoization (top-down) | Tabulation (bottom-up) |
|---|---|---|
| Approach | Recursion + cache | Iterative table fill |
| Ease of writing | Easier (mirrors recurrence) | Needs an explicit order |
| Subproblems computed | Only those reached | Usually all |
| Stack risk | Deep recursion can overflow | None |
| Space optimization | Harder | Easy (rolling array) |
| Time complexity | O(states * work) | O(states * work) |

sections.title: Memoization (top-down) - Fibonacci
Tabulation (bottom-up) - Fibonacci
When to Use Each
sections.content:
- **Memoization**: when the recurrence is natural and you want to code fast, or when **only a fraction of states** are actually reachable (sparse state space).
- **Tabulation**: when recursion depth could **overflow the stack**, when you need **space optimization** (rolling arrays), or for predictable performance with no recursion overhead.
- **Strategy**: derive the recurrence, code memoization first, then convert to tabulation if needed.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Memoization** = top-down recursion + cache; **Tabulation** = bottom-up table.
- **Same Big-O** time; differ in constants and space.
- Memoization computes only **reached** states; tabulation avoids stack overflow.
- Tabulation enables **rolling-array space optimization**.
- Code memoization for clarity, tabulation for performance/space.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Memoization and tabulation are two ways to implement the same dynamic programming idea, and they have the same time complexity, so neither is more real DP than the other; they just differ in direction and tradeoffs. Memoization is top-down. I write the natural recursive solution straight from the recurrence, and I add a cache, an array or a map, where I store each subproblem's result the first time I compute it. Before doing any work, I check the cache, so each subproblem is solved only once. The big advantages are that it's easy to write because it mirrors the recurrence, and it only ever computes the subproblems that are actually reachable, which helps when the state space is sparse. Tabulation is bottom-up. Instead of recursion, I figure out an order in which to fill a table, starting from the base cases and building up to the final answer iteratively. Its advantages are that there's no recursion, so no function-call overhead and no risk of a stack overflow on very deep inputs, and it often makes space optimization easy. For example, Fibonacci tabulated only needs the last two values, so I can drop the whole array down to constant space with a rolling pair of variables. So my practical strategy in an interview is: derive the recurrence, implement it with memoization first because it's quick and clear, and then, if I'm worried about stack depth or I need to reduce the space, convert it to a bottom-up tabulation, possibly with a rolling array.

speakable_v2.hook: Same Big-O, different personality - one caches a recursion on the way down, the other builds a table from the ground up and dodges stack overflow.

beats.text: Memoization is top-down recursion with a cache; tabulation is bottom-up iteration filling a table — both have the same time complexity, but in interviews start with memoization since it is easier to derive, then convert to tabulation if asked to optimise.

items: Memoization is top-down recursion with a cache

tabulation is bottom-up iteration filling a table — both have the same time complexity, but in interviews start with memoization since it is easier to derive, then convert to tabulation if asked to optimise

beats.text: Mention that memoization also incurs call-stack overhead (O(n) extra space) that tabulation avoids, and give a concrete interview strategy
candidates miss: Treating memoization and tabulation as having different time complexities — they solve the same subproblems and are asymptotically identical

speakable_v2.cap: Memoization is top-down recursion with a cache; tabulation is bottom-up iteration filling a table — both have the same time.
